paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

nodes.text: Does responsibility for rewards influence variations in happiness?
nodes.description: Whether rewards followed from the participant's own choices or their partner's choices affects how much those rewards influence the participant's happiness.
nodes.anchor: Crucial for our research question, we aimed to assess whether responsibility for these rewards, i.e., taking into account whether the rewards occurred following choices made by the participant or the partner, would also influence variations in happiness.

nodes.text: Does being responsible for low outcomes for a partner produce interpersonal guilt?
nodes.description: Participants feel worse when their own choice leads to a low outcome for their partner than when the partner's choice leads to the same outcome.
nodes.anchor: To specifically search for a sign of interpersonal guilt, we analysed happiness values reported after outcomes of lottery choices in the Social and Partner conditions

nodes.text: Which brain regions show activation reflecting interpersonal guilt?
nodes.description: The anterior insula becomes more active when participants are responsible for low outcomes that affect their partner.
nodes.anchor: To search for regions involved in this situation, we again analysed voxel responses using linear mixed models

nodes.text: Which brain regions are more engaged during social decisions?
nodes.description: Certain brain regions become more active when making decisions that affect both oneself and a partner compared to decisions affecting only oneself.
nodes.anchor: we aimed to identify the brain regions associated with social decision-making under risk, and searched for regions more engaged during decisions in the Social condition compared to the Solo condition

nodes.text: Which brain regions track consequences of one's choices for one's partner?
nodes.description: Brain regions respond more strongly to unexpected outcomes for the partner when those outcomes result from the participant's choices rather than the partner's choices.
nodes.anchor: We thus used this model to search for voxels responding more to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices

nodes.text: How does brain connectivity vary with social context and decision type?
nodes.description: Communication between brain regions that respond to guilt and responsibility changes depending on whether choices affect only the participant or both players, and depending on whether the choice is risky or safe.
nodes.anchor: We hypothesized that connectivity with regions that showed guilt- and responsibility-related responses during the outcome phase (see previous paragraph) might change depending on whether participants made decisions for themselves only or for themselves and their partner, and depending on the type of choice (Safe or Risky).

nodes.text: Study 1: behavioral study
nodes.description: Behavioral study outside the MRI scanner with 40 participants performing risky choice tasks in social contexts and reporting momentary happiness.
nodes.anchor: 40 healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22 to 31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

nodes.text: Study 2: fMRI study
nodes.description: Neuroimaging study with 44 participants performing the same behavioral task during fMRI scanning.
nodes.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23 to 50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study)

nodes.text: Ice-breaker game
nodes.description: A cooperative drawing game to create positive social bonds between participant and partner before the main task.
nodes.anchor: In this session lasting about 15 minutes, participants played an ice breaker game with their experiment partner, in which both participant and partner took turns in drawing one half of a simple picture while being blindfolded and following verbal instructions given by their game partner.

nodes.text: Risky decision task
nodes.description: Main experimental task where participants chose between safe and risky monetary options across three conditions (Solo, Social, Partner).
nodes.anchor: Following the icebreaker game, participants in Study 1 performed 3 sessions of a task in which they decided on each trial between a safe and a risky monetary option (Figure 1).

nodes.text: Risk premium estimation
nodes.description: Method to quantify risk attitudes by calculating the difference between lottery expected value and certainty equivalent.
nodes.anchor: Next, we estimated risk attitudes by calculating a risk premium for each participant and condition, defined as the difference between the expected value of a lottery and its certainty equivalent (positive values indicate risk aversion, negative values risk seeking).

nodes.text: CARA model
nodes.description: Expected utility theory approach using constant absolute risk aversion to estimate risk attitude parameter ρ from choices.
nodes.anchor: One simple model of risk aversion termed Constant Absolute Risk Aversion (CARA) assumes an exponential utility function:

nodes.text: Computational models of happiness
nodes.description: Five models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, Responsibility Redux) that explain happiness variations using rewards, prediction errors, and social comparisons.
nodes.anchor: Following previous work (Rutledge et al., 2014, 2016), we modelled the variations in momentary well-being (happiness ratings) using computational models that considered the influence of recent reward expectations, prediction errors resulting from those expectations, and differences in rewards obtained by the game partners.

nodes.text: Mixed-effects logistic regression of choices
nodes.description: Statistical model to test whether choices varied with expected value differences and experimental conditions.
nodes.anchor: we modelled choices with a mixed-effects logistic regression with subject-specific random intercepts u0j ∼ N(0, δu2) and slopes [u1j , u2j] ∼ N(0, δu2) and residual εij ∼ L(0, 1), assumed to follow the standard logistic distribution.

nodes.text: fMRI acquisition and preprocessing
nodes.description: Neuroimaging data collection using 3T scanner and standard preprocessing including realignment, normalization, and smoothing.
nodes.anchor: Imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens TRIO MRI system (Siemens AG, Erlangen, Germany) with a Siemens 32-channel head coil.

nodes.text: GLM1: event-related fMRI analysis
nodes.description: First-level GLM modeling brain responses to different trial events (choices, outcomes) across experimental conditions.
nodes.anchor: The first GLM (GLM1) included the following event types for each session: presentation of choice options, safe choice, risky choice (=lottery), receipt of outcome of safe option, all modelled separately for the Social, Partner and Solo conditions

nodes.text: GLM2: model-based fMRI analysis
nodes.description: Computational model-based GLM using regressors for certain rewards, expected values, and reward prediction errors from the best-fitting behavioral model.
nodes.anchor: In addition, we created another GLM (GLM2) with regressors designed to identify brain regions whose activation reflected the variables of the best-fitting computational model (see above).

nodes.text: PPI connectivity analysis
nodes.description: Psychophysiological interaction analysis to identify functional connectivity changes with insula and STS seeds during decision-making.
nodes.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox (McLaren et al., 2012) for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses.

nodes.text: Neurometric guilt signature comparison
nodes.description: Comparison of neural activation patterns with a published multivariate guilt-related brain signature from Yu et al. 2020.
nodes.anchor: As the GRBS and code to compare neural responses to it is freely available (https://github.com/canlab/Neuroimaging_Pattern_Masks/tree/master/Multivariate_signature_patterns/2019_Yu_Koban_Guilt), we compared this brain signature to the neural responses obtained in our task

nodes.text: Responsibility for rewards (whether rewards occurred following choices made by the participant or the partner) influences variations in happiness.

nodes.text: Participant happiness will decrease more following low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant rather than the partner chose the lottery (interpersonal guilt).
